VE.N.I.C.E PLUS ELECTRICAL AND ELECTRONIC SYSTEM GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS In conventional electrical systems, functions are activated with the aid of dedicated point-to-point connections. As the number of eletrical/electronic devices on board new vehicles has increased, the connection are becoming more complex and heavy. One reason for this is the complexity of functions implemented in the many electronic units, which require a continual interchange of data. All this makes it more difficult to install new electrical systems and increases the complexity of fault diagnosis. Many problems have been resolved and new electrical systems have been optimised compared to conventional systems by means of networking. This provides a more effective means of managing communication on board the car and for the transfer of information between subsystems via the serial buses present: single wires, pairs of twisted wires or even optical fibres. VE.N.I.CE (VEHICLE NETWORK INTEGRATION COMPONENT ELECTRONICS) ARCHITECTURE This is an application of the tried and tested multiplexing or (MUX) system The VE.N.I.CE PLUS system optimises the electrical system because each control unit is located in the centre of the functions it manages. This allows minimisation of the power and signal distribution system through the extensive use of serial communication networks. Power distribution takes place through junction units connected to the control elements (relays, actuators etc.) to ensure the maximum electrical protection and the minimum wiring complexity. The wiring architecture is reduced because each system function requires fewer dedicated cables because the wires (ABS, airbag, sidebag) are built into the front, facia or rear wiring harness. This also makes installation easier. Systems of this type offer innumerable advantates; for example: sensors in the various subsystems are made available to the network; information may be shared; similar sensors can be done away with; system flexibilty is increased; new functions can be added only by modifying the software (developed during the vehicle life), wiring design is simplified and the number of connectors is reduced, electronic device operating safety is increased to improve the reliability of information transmited, an integrated diagnostic function simplifies service operations on electric/electronic components. Tx - information to be transmitted to the nodes A (A1,A2) B (B1, B2) C (C1, C2) Rx - information received from nodes (B1, B2, C1) B (A1, A2, C2) C (A2, B1, B2) Classic solution The three control units (electronic nodes) require a number (N) of wires for each input/output in order to perform their function. This has created so much wiring that the system is more complex (design and manufacture), more bulky (weight, bulk and cost) and requires some 40 kg of wiring harnesses amounting to a length of more than 2 km. This requirement is likely to double every 10 years because even now one such vehicle may be equipped with 20 to 40 control units (ECUs). The first step that allowed us to reduce the volume and the complexity of the wiring harnesses was to group several electronic functions in a single unit: fewer control units = fewer wires. Examples of integration The engine control unit (NCM) manages injection, ignition, pollution system and engine cooling etc. 1 - Engine management control unit 2 - Engine cooling fan- first speed 3 - Engine cooling fan - second speed 4 - Injectors (injection) 5 - Coils (ignition) 6 - Lambda probe The multifunction control unit that manages: front window operation, door lock/release, timed passenger compartment and boot lighting, heated rear window timed activation and door mirror demisters. 1 - Multifunction control unit 2 - Door lock/release control unit 3 - Electric window control unit 4 - Timed front courtesy lights 5 - Timed luggage compartment light 6 - Activation of door mirrors and heated rear window for timed demisting The integration of electrical/electronic functions in a single electronic unit (ECU) has allowed us to improve: power consumption management (lower battery usage); functionality of appliances because they are managed by a single control unit; fault diagnosis due to control unit self-diagnosis. This first stage has allowed us to reduce the number of electronic units but not to reduce the volume of wiring harnesses sufficiently. Multiplexing solution Involves exchanging information between different electronic units on a single transmission channel (principle already used for the phone network, radio, TV etc.): 1 BUS (2 wires) for all information A-B-C - Nodes (ECU) A1-A2-B1-B2-C1-C2 - Communication bus D - Body Computer master control unit This second stage allows a decisive improvement because: Wiring is simplified and reduced Number of sensors is reduced (sharing of information) Electronic units communicate with one another. Obviously, the greater the number of systems requiring interconnection , the more attractive the MULTIPLEXING solution appears In general, in order to send data via multiplexing, we need to define the following with precision: transmission channel (wires, optical fibres, radio waves etc.); signal type on the channel (voltage, current, light etc.); communication protocol (all the rules that allow management of analogue or digital transmission management, code type, address, transmission order, error recording etc.). On our cars, the transmission medium or channel is a pair of wires known as a BUS. Under this system, packages of information are transmitted one after another without a set rigid sequence but according to the control units' needs). The signals are generated as voltages and the protocol used is CAN (controller area network), a system Robert Bosch in 1983 and has been developing ever since. Can (controller area network) network structure To allow the exchange of information, electrical/electronic systems in VENICE PLUS communicate via two physically separate networks known as low speed B-CAN and high speed C-CAN. Data to be shared between the B-CAN and C-CAN networksare managed by the Body Computer which acts as a system gateway because it is equipped with both interfaces. Via this device, two different network architectures are able to connect and convert certain application protocols into equivalent protocols in the other system. In practice, the body computer transfers information from the B-CAN (low speed) network to the C-CAN (high speed) network through the gateway and viceversa. Transfer may take place in two ways: directly: i.e. the entire message is copied to the other network exactly as it is; fragmented: i.e. the message received is broken down into its fields (signals) and recomposed as a new message by the other network. Connection of low speed can (b-can) In order to transfer information, all the electrical/electronic units are connected to the network via integrated, compatible interfaces in order to receive and transmit data. The B-CAN network (low speed) may feature up to 10 nodes (one per each control unit), all connected via a wire pair (CAN BUS). Maximum BUS length must not exceed 20 m and transmission speed is 50 kbit/sec. The communciation interfaces built into the electronic units for receiving and transmitting data are known as transceivers. The electronic units shown in the figure are connected to the B-CAN network (low transmission rate). 1 - Body Computer (NBC) 2 - Instrument panel node ECU (NQS) 3 - Climate control system ECU (NCL) 4 - Driver's door node ECU (NPG) 5 - Info-telematic node ECU (NIT) 6 - Radio receiver node ECU (NRR) 7 - Boot compartment node ECU (NVB) 8 - Termination resistances (incorporated) The network interface records overall and local faults; it avoids data loss in accordance with the following list of anomalies, which may be present on the B-CAN network Example: CAN wire or line (H) interrupted CAN wire or line (L) interrupted CAN wire or line (H) short-circuited to battery (+) CAN wire or line (L) short-circuited to battery (+) CAN wire or line (H) short-circuited to earth (-) CAN wire or line (L) short-circuited to earth (-) CAN wire or line (H) short-circuited to wire or line (L) The network interface loses any possibility of communication if both lines (H and L) are interrupted or if the two lines (H and L) are short-circuited and simultaneously connected to the car earth. Network termination/polarisation The termination resistances do not close the B-CAN line (H and L) like a loop but are connected directly to the CAN node, i.e. the transceiver of each individual ECU. High speed can (c-can) connection For the transfer of information, all electric/electronic units relating to the high speed C-CAN chain are equipped with a compatible interface for data reception and transmission. The C-CAN network (high speed) may serve up to 6 nodes (one for each ECU, all connected via a wire pair (CANBUS). Maximum BUS length must not exceed 10 m. Transmission speed is 500 kbit/sec. One fundamental requirement of C-CAN BUS wires is that they should be in plaited or twisted pairs. By winding two electrical wires into a plait or coil, the degee of immunity to electromagnetic interference of external origin is reduced. On the C-CAN network (high transmission speed), the following electronic units are connected to the Body Computer (NBC): 1 - Body Computer (NBC) 2 - Engine management ECU (NCM) 3 - Selespeed transmission ECU (NCR) 4 - Steering angle sensor ECU (NAS) 5 - ABS brake system ECU(NFR) 6 - 120 Ohm termination resistance on Body Computer and brake system node. The network interface cannot communicate at all if once of the following situations arises on the C-CAN network: interruption of one of the two lines (H and L) short-circuit between the two lines (H and L) short-circuit between one line (H) (L) on the battery (+), short-circuit of one line (H) (L) to earth (-). Termination/polarisation The termination resistances that close the C-CAN line (H and L) are present only in the Body Computer nodes (NBC) and brake system nodes (NFR). These take the form of two 120 Ohm parallel resistances on the BUS line that close to form a loop and thus create an impedence of 60 ohms (impedence seen from each node). Data transmission speeds are: B-CAN 50 kbits/s, C-CAN 500 kbits/s. The ECUs in the two CAN networks are programmed and operate by storage, processing and transmission of data and information by means of a binary convention, i.e. two symbols that refer to two basic electrical states: absence of voltage or presence of voltage; i.e. open circuit or closed circuit; i.e. level (0) zero or level (1) one Levels (0) and (1) constitute the basic information unit and are known as a BIT (binary digit). Binary ECUs use a binary language compatible with their electronic circuits (high low) (open closed etc.): data must therefore be handled in accordance with particular codes in order to transmit data. Various codes have therefore been developed to meet all requirements. One of the most common is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange). This alphanumerical code uses coded groups of bits and can represent the 26 letters of the British alphabet, plus the ten decimal figures in addition to punctuation marks and commands. ASCII is an eight-bit binary code. Seven bits are used to codet the information and the eighth is used to control errors. Using seven bits per character it is possible to code no fewer than 128 information items including decimal numbers, upper and lower case letters of the alphabet, punctuation marks etc.Once the number of bits in a word (i.e. the word length), has been fixed by a data code, this number must not be changed. A group of eight bits is known as a byte and represents no fewer than 256 values: this number is obtained by considering all possible combinations of (0) and (1) in the eight available byte positions, e.g. 00000001, 00001111, 11111111 etc. The number 256 (2 exp. 8) allows us to consider a set of alphabetical characters, punctuation marks, accented characters or special characters etc. In essence, a single byte may represent a number, a letter of the alphabet, a punctuation mark or a special character. The byte is used as a unit of measurement to describe quantities of data stored and storage capacity of storage devices. As with units of measure, byte are also defined as multiples: 1 kilobyte (kb) = 1024 bytes = 2 exp. 10 (2 10 ) 1 megabyte (Mb) = 1024 kb (about one million bytes)= 2 exp. 20 (2 20 ) 1 gigabyte (Gb) = 1024 Mb (about one billion bytes) = 2 exp. 30 (2 30 ) 1 terabyte (Tb) = 1024 Gb (about one trillion bytes) = 2 exp. 40 (2 40 ) Analogue: So-called linear electronics concerns analogue effects, i.e. that are proportional, continuous. A water tap is an example of an analogue switch because it can be used to shut off the water supply completely or turn it on fully, but can also be adjusted to all possible intermediate positions within the continuous range between closed and fully open states. The Tester mobile coil instrument is analogue: the needle can indicate the measurement position from zero to full scale deflection and also pass continuously along the graduated scale through all the points on its travel. It is often useful to determine a certain measurement by taking a value beween two marks on the scale within which the instrument pointer stops. Digital A digital electronic system proceeds in discrete jumps, i.e. quantifiable steps. A light switch is an example of digital operation because it can only take up well-defined, distinct states. Two in this case: on and off, without intermediate positions. In practice, a digital gauge with warning lights or numbers proceeds in steps and it is not possible to determine, for example, the exact level of a liquid between the state when the warning light is on and the state when the level gauge warning light is of. The sensitivity is therefore of the step due to the interval between one warning light and another but the reading is precise and not subjective. It is possible to place a series of steps between one warning light and the next with the same number of lighted indicators - and so until the measurement is taken in such small steps that it is almost the same as the continuum measured by the analogue gauge. The similarity is more apparent than real because each step travelled by the digital indicator, however small, determines a well-defined position and an unequivocal value that is above all not subject to reading errors of parallax or interpolation. To sum up, the sensitivity of a digital instrument is unparalleled and the reading precision is much higher. OPERATION OF THE MULTIPLEX NETWORK (VE.N.I.CE PLUS SYSTEM) In the VeNICE architecture, the system designers made the Body Computer responsible for control functions. The additional Body Computer functions provide information on: network activity status; the functional failure status of individual node ECUs; CAN network failure. The Body Computer node 'wakes the system up' when the ignition key is turned to MAR. In the event of an NBC failure, the network is woken up by the Instrument panel node (NQS) which intervenes only if the system is not woken up by the Body Computer for a certain time after the key is turned to ON to prevent network conflicts. Each 'Node' ECU processes the various signals from the respective sensors for their management and that of the other ECUs. For greater clarity, the following drawings illustrates a possible data sharing procedure between units connected in a network. In the latest generation of electrical systems a very high number of electronic units can be interconnected and a very high number of packages can therefore be handled. For this reason, these systems use one or more CAN networks which allow better information exchange between the various electronic units compared with conventional wiring. The physical medium used for the B-CAN network (low transmission speed) is a double copper electrical wire (not necessarily plaited) while C-CAN networks (high transmission speed) require a plaited wire; with one of the two wires associated with the high level (H) and the other with the low level (L). The CAN bus signals are differential, i.e. the value assigned to each bit is represented by the different voltage of CAN (H) and CAN (L). The combined use of two cables and differential signals allows data packages to be exchanged beween the various control units via the CAN network, even in the presence of electromagnetic interference. Transmission and exchange of data on the B-CAN and C-CAN and the transfer of information between a low speed network and a high speed network and vice versa takes place in the body computer node (gateway function). The teeth (maximum flow) and gaps (minimum flow) on the engine pulley toothed ring gear pass continuously in front of an rpm sensor to set up an emf or variable voltage pulses as indicated theoretically in the figure. In order to be used by the ECU microprocessor, the analogue rpm sensor signals must be amplified if they are weak (when ring gear speed is low or when the number of teeth is low) and converted to digital signals by means of a trigger circuit. The binary counter counts them: one pulse for each tooth. To prevent the numbering from going on to infinity, a time signal (clock) consisting of a transistorised circuit governed by a quartz every second restores the count to zero in order to start again. If we know the number of teeth on the ring gear, we can obain the crankshaft rotating speed. If a crownwheel has 240 teeth and turns at a speed of 1000 rpm, in one second 1000 ( 240 : 60 = 4000 teeth will pass in front of the sensor corresponding to 4000 impulses. If a binary counter clocks up 40000 impulses (bits) in a second, the crankshaft speed must be 1000 rpm. The speed will be higher than 1000 if it clocks up more than 4000 bits. The rpm reduced to digital form is one of the many information items used by the microprocessor (7) in processing data; In practice, a program stored in the control unit memories is able to convert the processing results into signals that act as inputs to the work circuits: injection base pulse constant, current intensity and duration in the coil primary winding, injection operation or the supply of other actuators designed for different functions; since this signal is destined to be used by other nodes, the engine control unit makes it available on the C-CAN network via its CAN node. In practice, the control unit converts the rpm signal into binary numbers - the only type that can be used by the microprocessor. They are then relayed to the CAN controller (10), which prepares a data package made up of different blocks or fields (contained between a beginning and an end) and represents an entire series of information to be sent to other nodes. The other interface, i.e. the CAN transceiver (11), decodes the package and sends it on the BUS network. In practice, it receives a series of pulses known as bits of value one (1) zero (0) that determine dominant or recessive voltage levels throughout the time the node transmits. All the other nodes that receive the package correctly confirm the reception (acknowledgement) on the BUS. All receiving nodes also carry out a test to check that the package (message) is relevant to them. Any node that finds relevant data in a package accepts it and processes it. Otherwise it ignores it. Communication protocol The circulation of transmission of a message known as a data package (frame) on a multiplexing network (B-CAN and C-CAN network) is possible only if a transmission protocol is adopted. This set of rules allows the exchange of information and commands between two or more electric units (control units or more accurately nodes). In practice, the communication protocol defines the structure of a frame and a frame obviously consists of a series of pulses (known as bits) that take a value of one (1) or zero (0). FRAME FORMAT 1 - Frame 2 - Blocks A - Identifies the start of transmission or the beginning of a new frame (START OF FRAME) SOF) consists of 1 dominant bit and indicates to all other interfaced nodes to be synchronised to this SOF bit (wakes up any BUSES that may be in stand-by mode). B - Identifier marks and identifies the content of a message. Also contains all information on message recipients. Arbitrage of the transmitted frame is carried out on this field. This means that the identification code uniquely identifies frame content and the priority assigned to it by the network architecture. (the lower the identification number, the higher the priority) C - Control field indicates frame or message structure D - Data to be transmitted (may be orders or information for transmission) E - Control field; checks that data transmitted are not altered (message validity). The node or nodes that first detect the presence of an error emit a series of dominant notification bits, the transmitter node eliminates the message and emits a new frame after a certain time. F- Reception confirmation (Aknowledment). All receiving nodes that use the message and have recorded the correct sequence from the transmitter node (recessive bit) overwrite the recessive bit with a dominant bit. In this way, the transmitting node is assured of correct message reception by at least one recipient. Each node checks the frame that it is receiving. If it finds it relevant, it accepts it and processes it. Otherwise it ignores it. G - End of frame, message terminated. The end of frame allows (if no node begins a new transmission to the network (BUS)) the system to enter a state of inactivity (IDLE) Management of priorities (superimposing or collision of non-desctructive frame) The VE.N.I.CE system protocol can deal with problems of superimposition when several nodes wish to issue a frame simultaneously. Each control unit possesses an identification code that is also an expression of its priority. In practice, when a node (control unit) expresses its intention to send a frame on the network (BUS) by means of its intial bit and another node (control unit) does the same thing simultaneously, because both read network signals (as well as transmitting them), the node that finds a difference between the emitted signal and received signal can tell if the other node is emitting a higher priority frame. A node sending a lower priority message interrupts its transmission immediately to make way for the node transmitting a higher priority signal. In practice, the higher priority message is sent via the network without any interruption or delay. Naturally, the control units (nodes) that intended to send messages with lower priority and had to interrupt transmission to become receivers, resume transmission of their own frames when transmission is complete. This non-destructive superimposition is regulated by means of an arbitrage bit: one is known as the dominant bit and its value is zero (0). The other bit is said to be recessive and its value is equal to one (1). This processes the signal from its rpm sensor to manage its functions and also sends it to the C-CAN network (high transmitting speed) to make it available to all control units (nodes) that are in listening mode. Each of these checks to see if the package is relevant to them. In this case, the receiving control units in listening mode that recognise information required to manage their functions are as follows: instrument panel mode (NQS), Selespeed control unit (NCR), climate control system control unit (NCL) and body computer node (NBC). The instrument panel node (NQS) uses this rpm information to govern the rpm gauge needle so that the driver can obtain information on engine rpm. The Selespeed control unit (NCR) uses the same information to manage and control gear changes by controlling clutch, gearbox and engine torque directly. (The interface between the Selespeed control unit (NCR) and engine control unit (NCM) improves system performance by relieving the driver of any need to synchonise accelerator clutch movements during gear changes that could be carried out with the accelerator pressed to the floor) The climate control unit (NCL) uses the same rpm information to manage activation of the supplementary heater (present only in JTD versions). In practice, the rpm information is associated with the battery charge status thus system voltage allows the climate control system (NCL) to keep up to date with engine conditions when the engine is running and whether the alternator is charging. If conditions are as specified,the 700W heater resistance circuit (PTC) can be supplied with power without problems. Once the data packages have been sent by the engine control unit (NCM), the control units in listening mode (NQS - NCR - NCL) execute the control within the required time. The body computer node (NBC) fitted directly into the facia control unit (CPL) manages many functions via microelectronics. Let's take a look at the heated rear window timed demist function as an example. The Body Computer (NBC) activates the supply to the heated rear window if: an INT signal is present (ignition key on), the facia control button connected to the climate control system ECU (NCL) is pressed (button pressed signal is sent to the body computer (NBC) via the CAN network. Automatic rear window heater element operation is dependent on the engine rpm signal. The following activation/deactivation strategy is applied: For the first 10 minutes, operation does not depend on the engine speed The next 10 minutes are dependent on engine rpm Engine rpm lower than 950 rpm: the rear window should go off after 10 minutes Engine rpm higher than 950 rpm: heated rear window should go on or stay on if already activated until it has been effectively working for 20 minutes. It may be deactivated during this period of automatic operation only if battery voltage drops below 8.5 V +/- 0.5 V. If the button on the facia is repressed for at least for at least 50 ms or if the key is turned off, the heated rear window is deactivated. Since rpm information from the engine control unit node (NCM) travels on the C-CAN network (high transmission speed) to reach the instrument panel node (NQS), which is connected to the B-CAN network (low transmission speed) it must be processed by the Body Computer (NBC) via the gateway function. Only after reprocessing does the body computer transfer the required information to the instrument panel node via the B-CAN network. (rev counter management) The interface between the engine control unit (NCM) and Selespeed control unit (NCR) is immediate because both are connected to the same CAN network. The other control units, which are not involved in the exchange of controls - e.g. the infotelematic or radio receiver node (NIT/NRR), that are in listening mode, read the information relayed down the BUS lines but do not process them because they are not essential for managing their functions. Serial line This dedicated serial line ensures data exchange between the various electronic units (nodes Essentially, the serial line is a copper wire used for consecutive data transmission by alternating high voltage levels (H) and low voltage levels (L) in continuation, i.e.serially. The figure above illustrates the High (H) and Low (L) voltage levels of the serial signal, i.e.: High (H) level: corresponds to a value higher than 80% of the battery voltage: logic level 1 Low (L) level: corresponds to a value lower than 20% of the battery voltage: logic level 0 Example: with a battery voltage of 12 V: High (H) level = > 9.6 V; Low (L) level = < 2.4 V. The data package communication protocol is defined by the baudrate, i.e. according to the number of bits (elementary message units) sent on the serial line in a second, i.e. baud rate The transmission speed is generally low (1000 baud rate = 10 kb/sec) Many information items are sent and mean response time is a few seconds. Control units connected to serial line k The control units connected to serial line K are shown below: 1 - Body Computer (NCM) front and rear view 2 - Airbag control unit (CAB) 3 - ABS control unit (NFR) 4 - Selespeed control unit (NCR) 5 - Electronic injection control unit (NCM) 6 - Serial line K Control units connected to dedicated lines (serial) The control units connected to dedicated lines are shown below. 1 - Body Computer (NBC) 2 - Volumetric sensor control unit (CAV) 3 - Antitheft siren control unit (CSA) 4 - Dedicated serial lines The serial line must be highly immune to electromagnetic interference. Each ECU is thus associated with a resistance and capacity circuit condenser that filters out interference. Trnasmission protocol Circulation of transmission of data packages on serial lines is possible only if a transmission protocol is adopted. This is the set of rules that permits the exchange of data and commands between the various electronic units (control units or nodes). Each control unit is connected to its own serial line and is identified by a different address so that data package transfer is unequivocal. Data package transmission takes place from a transmitting control unit to another receiving control unit and is thus one-way. This operation involves the dispatch of a question package, which is followed by a response package. The information flow does not therefore involve a question/answer type exchange. Data packages The data package format (A) is unique but composed of two main parts: control (B) and outcome (C). A - Package B - Command: represents information sent by a control unit and contains a command and relevant data/parameters. C - Outcome: confirmation of reception and execution of the command by the control unit to which it is sent. T - Time within which the control unit sends the outcome. Command format A frame (1) consists of several blocks (2) or fields: 1 - Frame 2 - Block A - 1 byte identifies the start of data transmission B - address of the recipient control unit (ECU) is inserted C - address of the sending (transmitting) control unit (ECU) is inserted D - identifies control sent E - identifies control data F1- F2...Fn - sequence of all data associated with the control G - Checksum (CKS) The command part contains a set of information expressed in bytes, namely: Section A (HDR) is the first package byte and identifies the start of the transmission. - It is used to wake up and sychronise the high control units and prepare them to begin receiving data or information packages. Section B (DEST) or 'destination indicator' identifies the control unit for which the data package is destined. It is possible to identify up to 60 control units connected on the line: each control unit is allocated a different address so that the data package transfer is unique. Addresses are assigned by the network architecture. Section C (MITT) sending control unit address. Identifies the control unit that sends the command (i.e. transmitting ECU). Section D (CMD) data for transmission. Identifies the command sent on the serial line. Up to 255 different commands can be identified and sent via the network. The command list is set by the network architect. Section E (NBD) number of control data bytes. Identifies the number of bytes in the command (CMD) sent on the serial line. Each command may be associated with up to 255 bytes of data that make up the parameters. The values that may be assumed by each command are set by the network architect. Section F1-F2...FN, identifies the (NBD) sequence associated with the command. Section G (CKS) or CHECKSUM is a check to ensure the data package has been received correctly. It is calculated as the sum of all data package bytes (from HDR to FN) Once data package reception is complete, the control units send the outcome to the transmitting unit. The outcome can be: ACK = command acknowledged and done NACK = command not acknowledged NAP = command not applicable Outcome format Once the command has been received, the receiving control unit (ECU) must send the outcome (within a specific time T) to the transmitting control unit to terminate the data package exchange. Bit 7 Bit 6 Bit 5 Bit 4 Bit 3 Bit 2 Bit 1 Bit 0 ESI_1 ESI_0 ECU BIT 7, BIT 6 - Identifies the true outcome BIT 5, BIT 4, BIT 3 - BIT 2, BIT 1, BIT 0 - identifies the address of the destination control unit (ECU). The outcome information indicates:: If BIT 7 is at level = (0) and BIT 6 is at level = (0) the command is acknowledged and executed. (because the commands and data received are correct and can therefore be executed by the control unit because it is one of its commands). (ACK) Ifl BIT 7 is at level = (0) and BIT 6 is at level = (1) the command is not acknowledged (because the command data received are incorrect) (NACK) If the BIT 7 is at level = (1) andBIT 6 is at level = (0) the command is not applicable (because although it has been correctly received and although it can be executed by the control unit because it is one of its commands; it cannot be executed with the control unit (ECU) in its current status Or it is not one of its commands (NAP). The combination BIT 7 level (1) and BIT 6 level (1) is not permitted The other six bits (from BIT 6 to BIT 0) identify the address of the command destination control unit and can therefore address up to 63 units. Serial line status During operation, the serial line can assume two distinct statuses: FREE LINE: identifies serial line resting state or free state, i.e. no transmission on the line. In this condition, the ECU can start transmitting. LINE BUSY: a transmission is in progress on the line. In this condition, each ECU (with the exception of the sender) stands by until the data package transmission ends. Access to the line (conflict in transmission) Two or more control units can begin to send information at the same time. This simultaneous access can create a conflict on the line; during transmission, the control units therefore check that every individual byte in the data package has been correctly sent. In practice, they check to ensure that what they have sent is the the same as what they have read on the line. If the comparison is negative, a transmission conflict has occurred. The transmission conflict immediately interrupts the data package transmission. Under these conditions, the control units immediately abstain from occupying the line for a set time (programmed) to ensure that all the other control units record the data package interruption. Once this time has elapsed, the transmitting control units consider the line to be free again and gain access to transmission using the priority mechanism. Access with priority Each control unit is allocated a priority access code (Pa) which determines the circumstances under which the control units give up the line after recording a conflict. (The priority standard is established by the network architect). In practice, any control unit (node) that is preparing to transmit, expresses its intentions to the other control units (nodes) by means of an initial bit. If two control units (nodes) carry out this operation simultaneously they do not realise immediately but as soon as a transmitting control unit (node) detects a dominant symbol on the BUS, it immediately suspends transmission of messages with lower priority to make way for the control unit (node) that is sending the higher priority message. In practice, the higher priority message is sent via the network without any interruption or delay. The control unit (nodes) that were intending to send messages with lower priority naturally interrupt their transmissions and set themselves to receive before re-attempting to send when the transmission is complete. Because the dominant level is the lower level, small identifier numbers indicate high priority messages. Access to the line after a conflict obeys the following rules: The control unit waits for a given time (programmed) after the conflict and declares the line free.. Once the line is fere, the control unit waits for a further period determined by its priority code before gaining access to the line. The line free condition does not herald the start of transmission but activates access with priority and transmission therefore starts. The transmission is carried out firstly by the control unit with the highest priority, which takes control of the line to prevent a new conflict. The other control units with lower priority codes that generated the conflict therefore switch to listening mode. Once the data package has terminated, they can attempt to regain access to the line in order to transmit the previously interrupted data package. Transmission of a data package Example of data transmission A - Package format B - Command: represents information sent by a control unit and contains a command and its parameter/data C - Outcome: confirmation of command reception and execution by the recipient control unit D - Free line T - Time (ms) within which the outcome must absolutely be sent Ta - time instant as a consequence of which a control unit with a higher access priority takes control of the line to prevent new conflict. Transmission of a data package between a transmitting control unit to the other control units connected to the network begins with the first byte (HDP) (this byte identifies the beginning and also wakes up the other control units at the beginning of package reception). It then continues with the command contents. Each control unit connected to the network swtiches to listening mode and determines, by means of the IND byte (address if the data package is addressed) At the end of command transmission, the receiving control unit processes it and transmits the outcoe. OUTCOME - YES/OUTCOME - NO If the control unit that permitted the command does not receive the outcome within the time required by the system, it considers that the command has not been sent and thus attempts to send the command again. It does not repeat the command if the outcome is received within the required time. A control unit in listening mode that identies a package not addressed to itself remains in listening mode until the end of data package transmission (i.e including outcome). The line is not occupied. The other control units consider the data package terminated when the time required for sending the outcome has elapsed. From that moment on, they can use the line to send new data packages.

COMPOSITION The diagram below illustrates the ignition switch. 1 - Ignition switch 2 - Ignition key 3 - Electrical connector a - INT b - INT/A c - POS d - PARK e - 50 f - 30 g - 15/54 OPERATION The diagram illustrates the connections. 1 - PARK: key can be removed from STOP to PARK by pressing the inhibitor button 2- STOP: key can be removed 3 - DRIVE: key cannot be removed 4 - STARTING: key cannot be removed automatic return to 'DRIVE' position The ignition key with a steering lock is a component which carries out the main function, through the insertion of a coded mechanical key, of supplying several circuits including the ignition/injection system, the engine starting and the services controlled by the ignition. The steering lock function is included amongst its tasks. The ignition key is equipped with an 'anti-repeater' device which prevents the starting manoueuvre if the key is not returned to the STOP position. The steering lock has two safety devices so that if one of them is broken and the ignition key is in the ON position the steering column cannot be mechanically locked. If the parking lights button is pressed it is possible to move from STOP to PARK and it is automatically released by turning the key to the STOP position. 1 - Aerial for ALFA CODE 2 - Aerial fitted on the switch The ignition switch is also used as a support for the aerial needed in transferring the codes in the ignition key transponder and is used by the ALFA CODE system for releasing the injection control unit (NCM) and allowing the engine to be started up. COMPOSITION The starting system consists of the ignition switch operated by the key and the starter motor which is connected directly to the battery. In addition to tried and tested starter motors which are energized in series and in series/parallel, for some time now starter motors are being developed which are energized by ceramic, ferrite type permanent magnets. CIRCULAR SECTOR MAGNET WITH MAGNETICALLY PRE-ORIENTATED CRYSTALS The rough components are formed into the desired shape by pressing and extrusion. Finally, after a thorough baking process, the material produces the mangets which are black in colour with a ceramic structure. The magnetizing treatment takes place during the manufacturing process. The magnets have a circular section and replace the polar section and winding. 1 - Radial orientation 2 - Parallel orientation STATOR-INDUCTOR The positioning of the magnets cannot take place using strong compression or riveting, also because the magnets are fairly fragile: they are secured by flexible fastenings and springs and, in some cases, they are stuck to the casing. The casing can be compared to a simple mechanical component without wires and is fitted using two stay bolts; it is equipped with 6 magnetic poles. 1 - N-S permanent magnets ROTOR-ARMATURE The diagram below shows the rotor-armature assembly. 1 - Shaft 2 - Ring gear 3 - Satellite/planet gears 4 - Pinion/sun gear 5 - Armature 6 - Manifold/switch Given that the magnetic field is created by permanent magnets, the energizing is the same in all motor operating conditions; in addition, as there are no energizing windings, there is neither an energizing current nor ohmic resistance: the total resistance depends solely on the armature circuit. The rotation speed is only affected by the current which passes through the blades and reaches the rotor depending on the voltage. Since the motor is equipped with permanent magnets, i.e. with fixed polarity, the direction of rotation depends on how the current is sent to the blades. When the rotor rotates it transmits movement to the three satellite gears on special supports which transmit their torque to the ring gear on the output shaft where the pinion which rotates the flywheel can be found. The optimum reduction ratio 1:4.26 is 4.26 revolutions of the rotor for each revolution of the ring gear and the presence of the permanent magnets makes it possible to construct motors of equal power from a simple design which are small in size compared with motors which have windings. COMPOSITION The alternator is a rotary machine which transforms mechanical energy into electrical energy. ALTERNATOR A127 IR-70/120A (INTERNAL VENTILATION) 1 - Rotor electro-magnetic circuit 2 - Assembly rods 3 - Rectifier side support 4 - Negative heat dissipation plate 5 - Positive heat dissipation plate 6 - Zener type pressfit power diode 7 - Manifold 8 - Regulation unit 9 - Heat shield cap 10 - Rectifier side bearing 11 - Rectifier side inner fan 12 - Stator electronic circuit 13 - Control side support 14 - Control side inner fan 15 - Control side bearing Like all electric machines, it basically consists of two parts: a rotor and a stator. The diagram below shows the rotor for an alternator with internal ventilation. Rotor The rotor is composed of a cylindrical magnetic core, concentric to the drive shaft, which has a toroid coil and two opposing magnetic impellers which are magnetized by the winding in the actual core. The impellers have six, claw-shaped, poles each, which interpolate reciprocally so that there are alternately six North poles and six South poles. There is therefore a single rotor winding which produces the e.m.f. for all the partial magnetic circuits. Stator The diagram below illustrates the stator. 1 - Star conection stator 2 - Triangular connection stator Stator This consists of a ring-shaped laminated group joined by two or more axial welding seams on the outside. It usually has thirty six grooves which contain the three-phase winding made from insulated copper wire with vinyl acetate and is connected, as necessary, by a star or triangular connection. RECTIFIER BRIDGE The diagram shows the rectifier bridge. 1 - Zener type power diode 2 - Dissipation plate 3 - Terminal B + alternator Bridge specifications The bridge consists of: Zener press-fit diodes. Diodes fitted on the dissipation plates electrically connected to the connection terminals with the phases. Dissipation plates. Large size dissipators. Phase insulation until the connection with the bridge through a rubber cable loom. Excess voltage limitation if the '+ battery' loads are disconnected guaranteed by the zener diodes. 1 - Normal diode 2 - Zener diode Zener diodes If the diodes are polarized directly they both allow the current to pass from the anode to the cathode (V+ I+): a zener diode therefore behaves like a normal silicon diode. If polarized inversely, initially the current does not flow from the cathode to the anode up to Vz (V-I-). Beyond Vz a normal diode is ruined, but a zener diode, on the other hand, continues to work normally because its resistance in these conditions decreases sharply. A zener diode is therefore a voltage stabilizer diode. On cars the voltage ranges from 4.7 to 24 Volt. It is one of the most important components in the regulation unit. It is often used for protection against polarity inversion or excess voltage. SPECIFICATIONS ALTERNATOR WITH INTERNAL VENTILATION SPECIFICATIONS The main feature of this type of alternator, with a 115 mm diameter stator, is having dual internal ventilation with the vanes inclined to guarantee the maximum flow of air and, at the same time, limit noise. Alternators with internal ventilation, for the same power supply, are smaller and lighter than types with external ventilation and satisfy all current application requirements (space in engine compartments is always at a premium). In addition to this, in terms of quality, these alternators are more reliable and durable than the best the competition currently has to offer on the market. In depth studies and research have made it possible to introduce all the devices, in production, designed to limit the noise produced by various components (fluid dynamics, mangetic, mechanical). In these conditions the energizing circuit (rotor) is enabled to earth by the regulator electronics. With the alternator rotating through the effect of the alteration in the number of revs and the mangetic field, a three-phase alternating volage is produced in the electrical circuit (stator) which, rectified by the diode bridge, can come out of terminal B+. When the upper fixed calibration level is reached (13.7 - 14.2 V) the battery is charged and the system supplied. The body computer checks the efficiency of the alternator recharging system by measuring two parameters: the voltage signal coming from alternator terminal D+ and the engine rpm signal received at the CAN network from the injection control unit (NCM). The lighting up of the warning light in the instrument panel (NQS) is determined by the levels recognized by the body computer being exceeded: in practice, if the voltage is too high (> 16.5 ± 0.5 V) or if the voltage is too low (< 7 ± 0.5 V) this causes the alternator to work irregularly in both cases with a consequent instruction by the NBC to light up the warning light in the instrument panel. If recharging signals are not present or irregular, carry out the following checks before dismantling the alternator: check belt tension; check the nut on the positive alternator terminal (B+) is tight and ensure the washer is present; check the nut on the excitation terminal (D+) is tight and ensure the washer is present; check that the nuts on the positive junction unit in the engine bay are tight; check the bolts securing the negative terminal to the body are tight; check the battery terminals are clean and fully tight; If the Body Computer does not provide the energizing signal, the alternator is energized at 1000 engine rpm (about 2200 alternator rpm) exploiting the residual magnetic field.

The function is activated: 1 - Within 2 minutes of a key off 2 - Operate the light flasher lever 3 - The dipped headlamps come on and their operation is signalled by the side lights warning light in the instrument panel (NQS) coming on 4 - Each time the flasher lever is operated, the time the dipped headlamps remain on is increased by 30 seconds. SPECIFCATIONS GAS DISCHARGE HEADLAMPS Introduction The lights play an important role among the vehicle's active safety systems. The need to improve the performance of current systems, based on halogen lamps, in terms of light energy emitted, spectral range and bulb duration has led to the technological development of gas discharge headlamps and the relevant devices which permit their operation on the vehicle. Three main advantages have resulted from the development of this technology: more efficient brightness permits a reduction in electrical energy when in steady state; the high light emission allows the size of the lights cluster to be reduced (particularly the height) offering greater freedom of design of the front; on average, the life is double that of a halogen bulb. The gas discharge headlamp technology has led to the development of a set of devices which, in short, comprise: xenon bulb; reflecting surface of the headlamp; control electronics, consisting of a reactor (igniter) and control unit (ballast); automatic light beam adjustment Light beam (isolux curve) of conventional headlamp Light beam (isolux curve) of discharge headlamp COMPLETE LIGHTS CLUSTER Each lights cluster contains the components necessary for the operation of the discharge lamp (bulb, reactor, control unit, control motor); the conventional components are also present (side lights, direction indicators, fog lights, main beam). Cross section of headlamp showing the gas discharge bulb 1 - Main beam 2 - Side light 3 - Gas discharge bulb 4 - Fog light bulb XENON LAMP The xenon lamp comprises a bulb containing two electrodes a few millimetres apart, and filled with xenon gas at low pressure. The emission of light is brought about by the striking up of an arc between the two electrodes, which is maintained during the operation of the bulb; this process is similar to what happens in neon tubes in civil applications. Unlike neon tubes, however, in an automobile application, however, it is unthinkable to have to wait for some minutes before the process stabilises, so the lights cluster has an electronic control device which permits operation, with regard to warm-up time, comparable to conventional headlamps. REFLECTIVE SURFACE The xenon bulb requires a new reflective surface, as the light emission point is shaped and positioned differently compared to the halogen bulb. The reflector used is of the complex surface type, so with no spherical lens. This surface receives light beams coming from the bulb and orientates them so as to provide a correct light beam distribution. Control electronics Each bulb is controlled by electronics consisting of two devices: the control unit (ballast) and ignition reactor (igniter). The purpose of the ballast is to convert the low-voltage direct current coming from the vehicle's battery into medium-voltage alternating current, and to control the subsystem's operation in closed loop. The ballast is thus able to control in an optimum way the characteristic voltage-current in the ignition stage, and can deliver to the bulb the power required to for operation in steady state. The igniter is controlled by the ballast and can generate the high voltage (max 25 kV) necessary for striking up the arc between the electrodes. The ballast in the left headlamp acts as 'MASTER': it receives the signals from the sensors, processes them and re-transmits them also the ballast of the right 'SLAVE' headlamp. Wiring diagram The figure shows a general diagram of the electrical connections A, MASTER headlamp B, SLAVE headlamp Sa, Front sensor Sb, Rear sensor DIA, Diagnostic socket Operation The operation of a xenon bulb is divided into four phases Ignition In this stage, the ballast generates a voltage which can strike up a specific device located in the igniter. A voltage step-up circuit transfers the overvoltage, suitably amplified, to the lamp, thus causing a discharge between the electrodes. Maintaining the arc (take-over) During this stage (a few seconds), the bulb is supplied with extra power which is necessary to cause the rapid evaporation of the metallic halides contained in the bulb, so as to quickly reach the brightness steady state. Under these conditions, the lamp emits a flash of light of double the normal intensity for a period of about 100 microseconds. Warm-up For a period of about two minutes, the ballast regulates the light intensity by measuring the physical state of the bulb from its impedance characteristics (closed-loop check). Steady state The light beam is continuously checked in closed loop even in steady state conditions. 1 - Supply (12 V) 2 - High-voltage generator 3 - Square-wave generator 4 - CPU 5 - Voltage step-up circuit A. Ballast B. Igniter C. Bulb Automatic headlamp alignment adjuster Because of the brightness of the beam emitted by the bulb, the vehicle must have an automatic headlamp alignment adjuster to avoid dazzling oncoming vehicles because of changes in alignment. The device intervenes in certain conditions: static type, due to load distribution; dynamic type, due to acceleration and deceleration. The automatic adjuster also ensures greater driving comfort, as the lit area remains stable and the eye does not have to constantly adapt to variations in illumination. The device comprises: a stepper motor for each headlamp; two load sensors, connected to the front and rear suspension, right side. Adjustment This is achieved via the signal of the load sensors which, connected to the suspension, give an indication of the vehicle's load condition. The control unit is 'activated' whenever the ignition is turned ONand resets the headlamps to the corrrect hight (calculated in relation to the vehicle load), which consists of the full tilting and subsequent positioning of the reflector. The signals of the load sensors are periodically acquired and suitably averaged so as to proceed, if necessary, with an adjustment of the headlamp position (e.g. fuel consumption during driving). This adjustment is not immediate, but is filtered over time to avoid unwanted adjustments (e.g. potholes, rough road surface, etc.). This adjustment is also carried out when the lights are off, so that the beam is correctly positioned the moment when the lights are switched on. Load sensors The sensors are fixed to the vehicle body, while an appropriately shaped lever follows the movement of the suspension. The sensor is supplied by the headlamp control unit, and supplies as an output a linear signal proportional to the position of the suspension in relation to the body. A - Part secured to the body B - Part secured to the suspension lever a - Angle of inclination of the lever V - Voltage of sensor's output signal Adjustment actuator A stepper actuator inside the lights cluster carries out the adjustment. This consists of a stepper motor and a screw-nutscrew reduction gear, which transforms from rotary into linear the motion of a pushrod hinged via a spherical ball to the reflective surface. 1 - Stepper motor 2 - Manual headlamp adjuster Self-diagnosis The electronics which manage the system include a self-test function which continuously checks its operation. The control unit carries out a continuous autodiagnosis of the system operation. In particular, it detects and memorises any faults. Faults stored in the control unit memory can be analysed by the Examiner or other diagnostic instruments. Recovery The self-test management logic also has the 'recovery' function: if errors are detected, the system no longer works correctly, and so incorrect orientation of the light beam could dangerously dazzle other vehicles. The light beam is then positioned low so it cannot dazzle under any circumstances, but permits sufficient illumination for safe driving to a garage on the Service Network. Zeroing In the case of replacement of a component in the system (headlamp, sensor, etc.), it is necessary to connect up the diagnostic instruments and carry out a self-learning procedure, to automatically reset the system, which must recognise the headlamp correctly algined position (position '0') from which it must make the appropriate adjustments.

SPECIFICATIONS INTRODUCTION The instrument panel on the 147 is fitted in the B-CAN network and takes the name NQS (instrument panel connector) The signals involving the systems in the C-CAN network are available to the NQS from the Body Computer connector via an interface known as a Gateway. The task of the NQS is to the display the vehicle operating parameters and inform the user of possible failures in the electronic on board systems. There are two basic versions of N.Q.S. the LOW LINE type N.Q.S. and the HIGH LINE type N.Q.S. The diagnostic socket is located in the EOBD, the dialogue line consists of the B-CAN line. The following operations can be carried out through diagnosis: Display of possible errors in the instrument panel Programming milometer mileage Setting mileage for SERVICE function (replacing instrument panel) Active diagnosis in order to check the operation of the instrument panel When the panel is replaced, the PROXI alignment must always be carried out (using the specific programme), if this is not done, the milometer will flash and the panel will not be fully operational. COMPOSITION The N.Q.S. consists of: Instrument panel on suitable versions in front of the driver with B-CAN interface MODE buttons (mode+ and mode-) in the left panel on the driver's side Km zeroing button, in the left panel on the driver's side Front headlamp adjustment button, in the left panel on the driver's side Trip Computer zeroing button, on the right wiper lever OPERATION The task of the instrument panel connector is to: Receive and transmit information at the B-CAN network Manage the subsiduary functions Receive and manage signals outside the network Display the vehicle operating stage The diagram illustrates the main connections for the Instrument Panel Connector The instrument panel connector functions are listed below SPEEDOMETER The speedometer shows speeds of between 0 km/h and 240 km/h. The scale is in km/h, on variants which have an imperial system there is a dual scale. The instrument panel receives information concerning the speed expressed in km/h via the B-CAN line and then displays it using the index which is moved by a P/P motor The speed information comes from the NBC, which calculates the speed using the wheel rpm signal from the NFR (ABS) and the measurement of the wheel circumference memorized in the NBC For speeds of between 0 and 4 km/h, the index remains stationary i the rest position. At higher speeds, the speed is signalled. Programming in 'miles' The NQS has a correction factor for the display in MPH which has been inserted by the manufacturer and cannot be modified. Error conditions In the case of an error, the speedometer indicator is positioned at zero (rest position) and remains in that position as long as the fault persists. Speed limit (high-line version only) On the High Line version instrument panel a speed limit can be set, using a Menu, with a range of between 30 - 250 km/h 920 - 160 mph) in steps equal to 1 km/h (1 mph). The limit selection is closed circle (no continuous rolling: when the limit is reached it returns back). When the selection has been made, with the function activated, if the speed of the vehicle exceeds the pre-set limit by + 1 km/h, a warning message is displayed on the matrix showing the + symbol and an acoustic warning is sounded (Alarm beep 1). The alarm signal remains activated (message up to a maximum of 20 s, after which only the symbol remains) until the vehicle speed is 5 km/h below the speed which activated the alarm EXAMPLE If a speed limit of 170 km/h is selected, the signal (message + symbol + alarm beep) is activated when the speed of the vehicle reaches 171 km/h and is deactivated when the speed is 166 km/h. Speed limit for arab market Irrespective of the speed limit set by the customer, for Arab markets there is a warning, signalled by the matrix display, for a speed limit of 120 km/h. If the function (set by the manufacturer at the end of the line) is activated when the vehicle speed exceeds the limit of 120 km/h by + 1 km/h, then the matrix display shows the warning message + the special symbol and an acoustic signal is emitted (Alarm beep 3). The alarm signal remains activated (message up to a maximum of 20s after which only the symbol and the auditory alarm remain) until the vehicle speed is 4 km/h below the speed at which the alarm was activated. MILOMETER The display has 7 segments and is configured almost like a DOT matrix in order to produce a similar configuration to the matrix display on the HIGH LINE type panel. The panel receives information, from the B-CAN line, concerning the space travelled processed by the NBC and information coming from the NFR and increases the milometer and the trip meter The km travelled are displayed in an LCD (1) which also displays information concerning the headlamp alignment. The light in the display is green and is produced by an SMD LED. The LCD has 6 digits (with 7 segments for each digit) for the 'total' figure and 4 digits plus a decimal point for the 'partial' figure. The zeros which are not important are not displayed in order to restrict the numbers illustrated to the significant ones. By pressing the 0 km' button (outside the NQS) for 1x < t < 3 x the partial counter is zeroed, but the mileage counter is not, nor the trip distance, nor the Service mileage. The instrument memorizes the total km so that if the battery (+30) is disconnected no more than +/- 1 km is lost. whilst for the partial mileage counter, the total memory is lost. The instrument is supplied by the factory with the possibility of resetting the total mileage counter only once during the first 200 km (or 125 miles). The possibility of this zeroing is shown on the LCD by the letter 'H' at the first digit (7 segments) on the left. If the operation described previously is carried out before 200 km is reached, the total mileage counter is zeroed (the partial mileage recorder is zeroed, the Trip meter is zeroed, the Service mileage is zeroed) if the '0 km' button is pressed for t > 10 s the letter H disappears. If this operation is not carried out when 200 km is reached/exceeded, the letter H disappears and the km travelled are maintained and displayed and the possibility of zeroing the total mileage counter is lost. The instrument allows the programming of the total number of km (if it is replaced) on condition that the figure entered is higher than the last figure memorized. When the maximum mileage is reached by the total mileage counter (699999 km - 399999 miles) it is not zeroed but horizontal bars are displayed. When 999.9 km is reached, the partial mileage recorder returns to 0.0 Milometer behaviour with key switched off Nothing is visible on the display with the key switched off; in this case the 0km button has no function. when one of the front doors (left/right) is opened/closed, the milometer display lights up and displays the partial and total mileage information for around 10 seconds. Programming in miles The unit of measurement for the total mileage counter cannot be modified through the set up function, it remains on what was set by the manufacturer. Error conditions In the case of an error, the milometer displays the last valid figure until it receives a new valid figure. REV COUNTER The rev counter shows figures of between 0 and 8000 rpm (petrol engines) and between 0 and 6000 rpm ( JTD engines). The panel receives information, via the B-CAN line, concerning the engine speed supplied by the NCM and displays it through a pointer moved by a P/P motor. The panel processes the engine rpm data without corrections with a constant time of 200ms so that the response at zero RPM - end of scale RPM is less than 2 seconds Position of index at key off At key off the index is positioned at 0 (0 rpm). Error cases In the case of an error, the index is positioned at ZERO (start of the scale) until the error condition disappears. Alarm signals If the indicator reaches the red danger zone, if the panel is partly lit, then the brightness increases. Engine coolant overheating warning light The panel receives information, via the B-CAN line, concerning the switching on/off of the warning light. The sofware strategy which regulates the switching on/off of the engine coolant temperature overheating wrning light and the operation of the pointer at the end of the scale when the temperature limits/levels are reached, both for normal operation and in the case of bursts of heat, is located inside the engine management control unit. Diagnosis / error conditions At each key on the instrument panel warning light is activated (check stage); after a time of t 4 s. the CCM/NCM sends the instrument panel the instruction to switch off the warning light. During this check stage the behaviour of the pointer should be as defined in the previous paragraph ('pointer behaviour at key on'). Through the effect of the warning light coming on, the pointer is not positioned at the end of the scale during the check stage. If the ignition is switched on and the conditions for switching on the warning light exist (engine coolant overheating and warning light already on when the ignition was switched off previously), then the CCM keeps the command to switch on the warning light activated and the instrument panel continues to keep the warning light on and position the pointer at the end of the scale. ENGINE OIL LEVEL GAUGE (only for JTD engine) The function of signalling the engine oil level is designed to show the status of the engine oil level during starting by means of a display. The instrument is equipped with a special circuit for the operation of a hot wire oil level sensor. The display takes place: on the LOW LINE version in the (milometer) disply and on the HIGH LINE version in the reconfigurable matrix display. Milometer display signal At the key on, the word 'OIL' is displayed in the lower part of the milometer for 10 seconds and the quantity of oil present in the engine is shown in the upper part by six digital squares lighting up/going out. With all the 'squares' lit up, the oil level is maximum. The squares in the upper part gradually going out indicates a decrease in the oil level. When the oil is at the minimum level, the squares in the upper section are all off and the dashes underneath flash at a frequency of 0.5 Hz. If the oil level is above the critical value, beyond the maximum level, the words 'HIGH OIL' are displayed for 10 seconds. if there is a break or a short circuit in the detection circuit at the key on, then the word 'OIL' flashes for 10 seconds at a frequency of 0.5 Hz and the dashes disappear. Reconfigurable matrix display signal The operating logic is the same as the one described for the LOW LINE except for the display mode. The display at the key on is defined as at MMI. After the measurement, the references are lit up with the same logic as the 'o's on the LOW LINE version. If the oil level is below the minimum level, the bars are all switched off and the 'minimum oil level' message is displayed for 10 secs., also all the bars are empty and the insufficient oil level symbol appears in the special warning light area. If the oil level is above the maximum level, the bars are all lit up and the 'maximum oil level' message is displayed for 10 secs. If an oil level sensor failure is detected, the message 'oil level sensor failure' is displayed for 10 secs. Acquisition of the signal The counter is zeroed when the battery is initially connected. At the first key on, the oil level reading is taken (time - 1 sec.) and the result is shown on the display. After the reading the counter is set at 20 minutes. During the key on period the counter decreases by one unit per minute up to a minimum value of 2 minutes. At the next key off the counter decreases from two to zero. At the next key on and, only if the counter is at zero, the system reads and memorizes the new value. If the counter is still >0 at the key on, a comparison is made with the previous reading and, if: the current reading is greater than or equal to the previous one by 3 segments, effective references of the display, the value read is acquired and memorized and the counter is reset at 20 starting the decrease as previously; the current reading is less than 3 segments, effective references of the display, the reading is not memorized and the level corresponding to the previous reading is displayed. The counter is reset at 20 starting the decrease again. The aim of the system is: to monitor the efficiency of the system; to signal an increase in emissions due to a vehicle malfunction; to signal the need to replace deteriorated components. Prompt repair of the problem which has caused the warning light to come on is vital in accordance with the legal requirements of the traffic regulations of the country in question. CLOCK/DATE Specifcations The clock is shown in the DISPLAY (2), namely in the segment LCD on the LOW version and in the matrix display on the HIGH version. In 24 h mode, the reading is in hours and minutes and ranges from 0:00 to 23:59. In 12 h mode, the reading isin hours and minutes and rages from 1:00 to 12:59; the 'AM' reading changes to 'PM' when the clock moves from 11:59 to 12:00 during the day and conversely the reading changes from 'PM' to 'AM' when the clock moves from 11:59 to 12:00 at night. Each time the battery is reconnected or the process reset, the clock shows 0:00 (or 12:00 in 12 h mode) and the two points between the hours and minutes flash at a frequency of 0.5 Hz - DC 50%. Clock adjustment By pressing the 'mode' button the hours/minutes flash at a frequency of 0.5 Hz - DC 50%. The buttons (+ e -) are used to adjust the hours as follows: Pressing the button for < 0.05 secs, nothing happens Pressing the button for between > 0.05 secs and < 2 secs, the digit changes by 1 step/sec Pressing the button for between < 2 secs and < 4 secs, the digit changes by 5 steps/sec Pressing the button for > 4 secs, the digit changes by 10 steps/sec When step 5 or 10 is activated, the figure moves to the next value which can be divided by 5 or 10, respectively. Pressing 'mode' changes from hours to minutes and the same method for correcting the hours can be used to change the minutes. When the 'mode' button is pressed again, the adjustment is accepted and the minutes stop flashing. During the adjustment of the hours/minutes, the seconds return to zero to confirm the figure set. The digits (:) do not flash during the modification; the digits (:) start to flash when the adjustment is confirmed. If not button is pressed during the adjustment for 10 secs, the instrument moves on to the standard screen without accepting the last setting made and the previous time is displayed. The adjustment buttons (Mode, +, -) are outside the panel. The NQS reacts to the pressing and not the release of the button. The clock is only displayed with the ignition switched ON. The time can only be set/adjusted with the ignition switched ON and the vehicle speed below 3 km/h. Clock (low line) The 12 h mode is only activated by the supplier and cannot therefore be adjusted by the customer. 'AM' or 'PM' are not displayed in this mode. To enter the clock set up mode, press the 'mode' button. Clock (high line) The 12/24 h mode is activated through the menu and can therefore be adjusted by the user. 'AM' or 'PM' is shown in the 12 h mode. To enter the clock set up mode, press the 'mode' button. The summer/winter setting can be selected using the menu. Changing from OFF to ON adds 1 hour (summer-time activated). Changing from ON to OFF subtracts 1 hour (daylight saving time activated). Data (high line only) The date ranges from 1999 to 2099. The format is represented on the display in DD MM (day, month) The indication of the year in progress is not displayed. Leap years are calculated automatically. When the date is being updated, impossible dates are not represented.for example for a month with 30 days, the 31st cannot be displayed. Inertia switch intervention signal At each key off the inervention of the inertia switch is signalled to the user. This signal is shown on the display 2 until the switch is reset manually. The segment display (LOW line) shows the warning 'FPS on' flashing at a frequency of 0.5 Hz d.c. 50% on (FPS = Fire Prevention System). The matrix display shows the warning 'Inertia switch on' + symbol At the key off the state of the switch is acquired for a maximum of 30 seconds. For the High line version: speedometer graphics lighting (activated only by the +lights signal) graphics lighting: fuel gauge, engine coolant temperature gauge, rev counter, (activated only by the +lights signal) milometer display (1) lighting matrix display lighting. (2) --> main information / messages area. matrix display lighting. (2) --> area dedicated to warning signals. The graphics are lit in red. The milometer (Low and High versions) and clock/text displays (Low version) are lit in red. The matrix display is also lit in red for the information/message display area; the 32 x 32 pixel area (bottom right) is lit in green, red or yellow (for the ideogram warning lights). Operation The LEDs are activated when they receive the 'side lights on' signal from the NBC via the B-CAN line. The instrument can activate the LEDs when the NQS is separated from the B-CAN (with the + of the headlamp alignment corrector). The panel lighting can be deactivated, with the sole exception of the speedometer scale (for the High Line version only). For a partial deactivation, (with the side lights on), press the 0Km' button for 4 < t < 10 secs (the partial mileage counter is not zeroed in this case) (N.B.: time greater than partial zeroing). If one of the readings not lit up enters the warning stage (e.g. fuel reserve, engine coolant temperature > 100° C, engine speed at the start of the red sector, DOT matrix warning) the entire panel will be lit up and remain activated until the warning stage is over. After the key on and the +lights on, the entire panel lighting will remain activated. HEADLAMP ALIGNMENT ADJUSTMENT The headlamps can be adjusted from 0 to 3 usig the '^' and 'v' buttons (outside the panel in the left panel); the value set is memorized and shown in the milometer display together with the symbol. The NQS receives and sends the increase signal (CAF+) or decrease signal (CAF-) from the switch in the left panel to the headlamp adjustment module (incoroporated in the actual NQS). The adjustment module controls the presence of the positive headlamp supply coming from fuse F13 and produces an adjustment signal, sending it to the headlamp aglinment control motors electronic circuitry. The instrument output signal is a voltage value which is interpreted by the actuator fitted on the headlamp; No adjustment is possible at the KEY OFF. At the KEY ON the last value memorized is maintained, but the number and the symbol are not displayed in the panel until the dipped headlamps come on. The prolonged operation of the button does not lead to a gradual adjustment. Disconnecting the battery or resetting the system causes the value memorized to be lost. After resetting the system starts again from zero (default value). ACOUSTIC FUNCTIONS Specifications There is a buzzer in the NQS which emits the following auditory signals. Button operation: confirmation that one of the buttons has been operated known as a roger-beep. The NQS receives a signal that the roger beep has been activated from the other connectors via the B-CAN network The following buttons produce an auditory signal: front electric windows controls left panel controls centre panel controls with the exception of the HAZARD button climate control controls Signal for the following types of alarm: Alarm beep 1 Alarm beep 2 Alarm beep 3 The NQS manages the type of alarm according to the signals coming from: B-CAN network systems connected directly to the panel functions inside the panel The NQS produces the corresponding auditory signal as described below. The buzzer management logic is as follows: roger-beep: frequency 1.5 kHz, duty cycle 50%, duration 50ms alarm beep 1: frequency 4 kHz, duty cycle 50%, duration 2 s - modulation equal to 1Hz dc 70% alarm beep 2: frequency 4 kHz, duty cycle 50%, duration dependent on the function - modulation 2Hz dc 50% alarm beep 3: frequency 4 kHz, duty cycle 50%, duration dependent on the function The NQS manages the buzzer activation priorities, which are: Roger Beep: 3 Alarm beep 1: 2 Alarm beep 2: 1 Alarm beep 3: 0 MAXIMUM PRIORITY If there is a simultaneous request for several auditory signals, the one with the greatest priority only is produced; the others are aborted. Danger signals (high line & low line) The danger signals are: In the case of 'doors open' and if the speed of the vehicle is above 3 km/h for longer than 4 s, there is an alarm beep 2 type auditory signal. In the case of 'handbrake applied' and if the vehicle speed is other than zero for longer than 4 s, then an alarm beep 2 type auditory signal is produced. In the case of 'doors open' and 'handbrake applied' the signal is timed (about 10 secs) and only repeated at the key on If there are faults, an alarm beep 1 type auditory signal is produced. If the speed limit set using the Menu is exceeded, an alarm beep 1 type auditory signal is produced. If the speed limit defined for the Arab market is exceeded then an alarm beep 3 type auditory signal is produced. If the outside temperature is below a pre-set level then an alarm beep 1 type auditory signal is produced. Adjustment of buzzer volume On the LOW line version the buzzer volume (for the Roger Beep function) can be activated or deactivted by pressing the MODE button. On the High line version the buzzer volume can be adjusted to 4 different levels. For the Roger Beep function the buzzer volume can be adjusted from 100% to 0% as defined in the table; to signal an alarm, the buzzer volume can be adjusted to a mininum value of 10%, as defined in the table, even if the off level is selected.
